nameStory: Gray dogwood gets its name from its grayish-brown bark and stems, which stand out especially in winter when the leaves have fallen. Like other dogwoods, it belongs to a plant family whose hard, dense wood was once used to make "dags" or "dags" - sharp wooden skewers used for cooking meat.
description: Gray dogwood is a medium-sized native shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall and wide, forming dense thickets through underground runners. It has a somewhat scraggly, irregular growth habit with multiple stems branching from the base. The plant produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by white berries on bright red stems that are quite striking against the green summer foliage.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: White berries about the size of small peas sit on bright red or pink stems in late summer - this red-and-white combination is like nature's candy cane and makes gray dogwood unmistakable among shrubs

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves are oval-shaped, 2-4 inches long, with prominent curved veins that arch toward the leaf tip - run your finger along these veins and you can feel them clearly

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers cluster in flat-topped or slightly rounded groups about 2-3 inches across in late May to early June, with a faint sweet fragrance

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems are reddish-brown to gray with a smooth texture, while older bark becomes more gray and slightly rough to the touch

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading colonies through underground runners, creating dense thickets with multiple upright stems that have an open, somewhat irregular branching pattern

habitat: Gray dogwood thrives in a variety of conditions from wet to moderately dry soils, often found along woodland edges, in old fields, and near wetlands throughout New England. It's particularly common in disturbed areas and can tolerate both full sun and partial shade. You'll often spot it growing alongside other native shrubs like elderberry and native viburnums in transitional areas between forests and open spaces.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late April to early May, followed by clusters of small white flowers in late May to early June that attract various small pollinators.
seasonality.summer: White berries ripen on distinctive bright red stems from July through September, creating the plant's most recognizable feature while leaves remain green.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn purplish-red to maroon before dropping, while white berries may persist on their red stems well into the season.
seasonality.winter: Bare gray-brown stems show the shrub's irregular branching pattern, and some white berries may still cling to red stems, providing winter interest and bird food.

funFact: Gray dogwood berries are arranged on bright red stems that look exactly like tiny red coral - this isn't just pretty, it's strategic! The red stems make the white berries more visible to birds from a distance, essentially creating a natural "eat me" billboard that helps the plant spread its seeds.
confusionNotes: Gray dogwood is most often confused with silky dogwood, but silky dogwood has blue berries (not white) and prefers wetter conditions. Remember: gray dogwood = white berries on red stems, silky dogwood = blue berries.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "gray" dogwood, the most colorful parts of this plant are actually the bright red fruit stems and the white berries - the gray refers mainly to the bark color seen in winter.
compareHints: Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries. Gray dogwood also forms spreading thickets unlike the tree-form flowering dogwood or the wetland-loving red osier dogwood.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
